tip: Paired comparison uses 'ju ... desto', the more of one, the more of the other: 'ju mer du övar på att prata svenska, desto mer självsäker kommer du att bli'.
Mid-sentence adverbs like 'ofta' go between 'har' and the main verb: 'vi har ofta undrat', not 'har undrat ofta'.
Swedish uses the 24-hour clock for schedules, so 'avgår klockan 14:35' means departs at 2:35 pm.
A whole clause can fill the first slot: 'vad han sa' works as the subject, so the verb 'förvånade' comes right after it.
Front the object for emphasis and the verb stays in second place, so the subject 'jag' follows: 'henne har jag aldrig träffat'.
Front an infinitive for emphasis and the verb still comes second: 'springa' puts 'orkar' before the subject 'jag'.
The -s ending forms a passive: 'syns' means is seen or is visible, so 'jag syns inte' = I cannot be seen.
Opening with an adverb like 'sällan' (seldom) flips the order: the verb 'har' comes before the subject 'jag'.
The -s ending can mean each other: 'kramas' is hug one another, so 'vi kramas' = we hug each other.
'Torde' is a formal, mostly written helper verb for cautious probability: 'det torde vara möjligt' means it should presumably be possible.
When 'aldrig förr' comes first, the verb moves ahead of the subject: 'hade jag' (had I), not 'jag hade'. Swedish keeps the verb in second slot.
The -s ending makes a passive: 'presenteras' = are presented. This form is common in Swedish academic and formal writing.
The Swedish possessive is just -s with no apostrophe: 'sommarens dagar' means the summer's days. Do not add an apostrophe like in English.
For 'as X as', Swedish uses 'lika X som': 'inte lika vanligt som' = not as common as, with the adjective between 'lika' and 'som'.
'Tacka nej till' = to decline, 'tacka ja till' = to accept. The verb 'tacka' takes 'till' here, plus 'nej' or 'ja'.
Adding -s to the past tense (here -des) forms the passive: 'hördes' means was heard.
For reaching an age, Swedish uses 'fylla' (to fill): 'hon har snart fyllt tjugo' = she will soon turn twenty.
In a main clause a short adverb sits between 'har' and the main verb: 'har ofta besökt', not 'har besökt ofta'.
The -s ending makes a passive with no helper verb: 'barnbidraget betalas ut' = the allowance is paid out.
'Slå sig ner' means to sit down or settle in; 'sig' changes to match the subject: 'vi hade just slagit oss ner'.
For food and drink pairings 'till' means to go with: 'en kanelbulle till kaffet', a bun with the coffee.
When 'vad' is the subject of the clause that follows, add 'som': 'vad som kan hända' (what can happen), not 'vad kan hända'.
A length of time before a noun takes the possessive -s: 'fem veckors semester' = five weeks of vacation.
For completed actions Swedish uses 'har' even with motion verbs: 'jag har precis kommit hem', never 'är kommit'.
When a time phrase opens the sentence, the verb stays second, before the subject: 'den trettonde december firar vi'.
'Lär' plus a verb means is likely to or will probably: 'det lär dröja' = it will probably take a while.
'Blev' plus a form like 'försenat' marks a change that happened to the subject, unlike 'vara' which just states a fact.
'Hjälptes åt' uses the -s to mean each other, so 'hjälptes åt att bära' = helped one another carry, not a passive.
'Med facit i hand' literally means with the answer key in hand; it's the Swedish way to say in hindsight.
Add -s to make the passive: 'skrevs' = was written. The doer follows 'av', so 'skrevs av Astrid Lindgren' means written by her.
